description: TALEXIUS es una plataforma web hecha en Cajamarca para mirar el clima de todo el Perú en un solo mapa: los 25 departamentos y sus provincias, con datos abiertos de la NASA y del Perú, en español e inglés y de acceso libre. La estamos construyendo para que cualquier persona pueda ver cómo está su territorio hoy.
summary: TALEXIUS is a territorial sentinel for Peru. The problem: national climate alerts, whether for El Niño or La Niña, do not say which territory is in danger, and a rainfall total means nothing on its own, because 100 mm can be normal in one department and a disaster in another, just as a rainfall deficit can quietly become a drought. TALEXIUS compares NASA Earth data (rainfall, soil moisture and temperature) against each department's and province's own climate history since 1981. It reads both ENSO poles, El Niño excess and La Niña deficit, and shows a simple traffic light, Normal, Alert or Critical, a territorial risk level and how many people live in the exposed territory. It also has a live mode: today's weather for every department (temperature, rain, humidity and wind), next to the historical record. It is built for decision-making: INDECI, regional and municipal authorities and civil defence teams get a ranked list of where to act first, instead of a national average. It opens on the El Niño event in progress in 2025–2026, with the historical episodes of both signs one click away.
details:
Executive Summary

TALEXIUS is a public web sentinel that turns national climate alerts into a territory-by-territory action list for Peru. It reads rainfall, soil moisture and temperature against each territory's own history, across both ENSO poles: El Niño excess rain and La Niña water deficit and drought risk. It compares current conditions in each of the 25 departments and 195 provinces against that territory's own climate history since 1981, using NASA POWER data, and shows a simple traffic light with the exposed population. It is live at talexius.vercel.app and opens on the El Niño event in progress, 2025-2026, under an active official ENFEN alert.

1.1. What it does

TALEXIUS is a territorial sentinel for Peru. For each of the 25 departments and their 195 provinces, it compares current conditions against that same territory's own climate history and flags whether rainfall and El Niño are normal or dangerous right now in that exact place, and how many people are exposed. It serves regional and municipal authorities, civil defence teams and citizens who need to know where El Niño is dangerous right now. The sentinel is built for public decision-making: its intended users are INDECI, regional and municipal authorities and civil defence teams, who must decide where to act first when a territory shows excess rain or water deficit.

1.2. How it works

Rainfall, temperature and soil moisture come from NASA POWER (1981 to the latest available month). For each department and period, TALEXIUS computes the rainfall anomaly against the department's own historical distribution and shows a traffic light defined by standard deviation: Normal up to 1σ, Alert between 1σ and 2σ, Critical above 2σ. Risk is phenomenon × exposed population: each department card shows population, the period anomaly and people living in territory under alert. Episode windows follow the NOAA Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) and the Peruvian Coastal El Niño Index (ICEN). The system opens on the event in progress, El Niño 2025–2026, and allows comparison with past episodes such as the 1997–98 Mega El Niño, the 2017 Coastal El Niño and Yaku 2023. The official Peruvian context is ENFEN Official Communiqué No. 20-2026 (13 November 2026): the Coastal El Niño Alert remains active, of extraordinary magnitude until February 2027, with above-normal rain expected in the north-western highlands, including Cajamarca. ENFEN watches the ocean; TALEXIUS watches the territory.

1.3. Innovation and purpose

The innovation is the reference frame: a territory is never compared with a national average, only with its own history, which is what makes a rainfall figure meaningful. The purpose is decision support: converting a national ocean alert into a ranked list of territories with the exposed population attached to each one.

1.4. Benefits and impact

A. Social, environmental and technological benefits: social, regional and municipal authorities and civil defence can prioritise limited resources where the most people are exposed; environmental, earlier preparation reduces damage from floods and landslides during El Niño and from water deficit and drought during La Niña; technological, the system integrates open NASA Earth data, national statistics and official alerts in one public web tool. B. Contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals: SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities) and SDG 13 (climate action). C. Expected community impact: faster, better-targeted local decisions in Peru, starting with Cajamarca.

1.5. Objectives and expected results

Objective: a working sentinel that, for every Peruvian department, shows the current climate state against its own history, the exposed population and a risk ranking. Expected results: the live web application at talexius.vercel.app, department cards with anomaly, soil moisture, population and people in alert, and comparison between the current event and historical episodes.

1.6. Methodology and work plan

Phase 1 (Saturday morning): concept, challenge selection and data download (NASA POWER series, ONI episode windows, INEI population, ENFEN communiqué). Phase 2 (Saturday afternoon and Sunday): application build with AI assistance, live deployment. Phase 3 (Sunday): data audit of the live build against the sources, corrections, demo video and submission. Deliverables: the live application, this documentation and the 30-second demo video.

1.7. Methodology and tools

1.7.1. Tools and software: WebStorm IDE with Antigravity CLI (Gemini frontier models) for AI-assisted development, NASA POWER data services, Vercel for deployment, YouTube for the demo video.

1.7.2. Languages and frameworks: TypeScript with React 19 and Vite 7, styled with Tailwind CSS 4. The maps and charts are custom SVG components (no mapping library). The historical series were processed with Python scripts that download NASA POWER data point by point for each territory.

1.7.3. Hardware and sensors: none; the system works entirely with satellite and reanalysis data from NASA and official Peruvian sources.

1.8. Project management: team and roles

How we worked: the idea was shaped in the days before the event, and the team was formed in person at the Cajamarca venue on November 14: the project lead defined the concept and the architecture, the developer built the application, and our third member joined remotely with research and the El Niño framing. We worked in short iterations: first the concept and the territorial scope (Peru only, each territory against its own history), then the data pipeline from NASA POWER, then a number-by-number audit of the departmental and provincial figures against their sources, a visual pass over the interface, and finally the documentation and the submission. Decisions were reviewed together at the venue and over the team chat, and every figure the platform shows was verified against its source before the submission was closed.

Team roster and roles:

Edwar Jhanpiere Saenz Tello, project lead and architecture: concept, system architecture and key decisions, review of the build and its processes, verification and audit of every figure against its source, documentation and submission.

Edgar Mejía, software development: wrote the web application code, data download and processing pipeline, deployment.

Holy Lisbeth Campos Vásquez, research and presentation: research and ideas on the El Niño phenomenon and its importance, data review, presentation and demo video.

1.9. Location

Peru, national coverage at department level (25 departments) and province level (195 provinces), with Cajamarca as the home region of the team and the reference case for the current El Niño alert in the north-western highlands. Justification: Peru is one of the countries most exposed to El Niño, and the official alert is national and oceanic, while decisions are taken territory by territory; there was no public tool that translated the alert into local risk with exposed population, which is the gap TALEXIUS fills.

1.10. Impact and benefits: alignment with NASA

TALEXIUS is built on NASA Earth observation data (NASA POWER) and official Peruvian population data (INEI), applying them to climate resilience and disaster preparedness, in line with NASA's Earth science mission of using space data for decisions on the ground.

1.11. Expected results

A public, working sentinel for Peru that any authority or citizen can open and understand in seconds: current state by department, exposed population and a risk ranking, reproducible for future El Niño events.

1.12. Conclusions and future improvements

Lessons learned: a climate figure only means something against the territory's own history, and every number on screen must be verifiable against its source. Future improvements: district-level layer (Cajamarca has 127 districts), frost and wildfire views with NASA FIRMS data, continuous updates as new POWER data is published, and extension of the same method to other countries, with Peru as the pilot.

1.13. Annexes

Live application: https://talexius.vercel.app. Presentation (7 slides): https://www.canva.com/design/DAHbB-_zbgY/lCvHze5ukd8pwXdGZW1IVw/view .

PDF copy: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xlqWwDaTP3LArj5aSTX3cJCZYy9bv2w/view. Demo video: the YouTube link in the Project Demonstration field. Photos of the team at work during the Cajamarca event, and a PDF copy of the presentation, are in the shared evidence folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1DZ0_YkzAwIdFrXl-9v4XuklCRHBnx2o8. References: NASA POWER, https://power.larc.nasa.gov/ ; NOAA Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/ensostuff/ONI_v4.shtml ; IGP Coastal El Niño Index (ICEN), https://www.igp.gob.pe/ ; ENFEN Official Communiqué No. 20-2026, https://enfen.imarpe.gob.pe/downloads/comunicados/ ; INEI population projections 2024, https://www.inei.gob.pe/ ; Open-Meteo API, https://open-meteo.com/ ; tools: WebStorm, https://www.jetbrains.com/webstorm/ , Vercel, https://vercel.com/ , Canva, https://www.canva.com/ .

Use of AI

TALEXIUS was conceived, designed and directed by the team: the concept, the territorial approach, the choice of data sources and every decision about what the system shows are ours. AI assistants were used as coding tools (Antigravity CLI, whose models are Google's Gemini frontier models, inside the GitPod code editor) to build the web application under our direction, with human review of the code and verification of every figure against its source. All data shown comes from the named sources (NASA POWER, NOAA ONI, ENFEN, INEI); no climate figure was generated by AI.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources), https://power.larc.nasa.gov/ : the backbone dataset of TALEXIUS. We use four variables, rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), temperature (T2M, T2M_MIN, T2M_MAX) and root-zone soil moisture (GWETROOT), from 1981 to today, in two ways: (1) historical series downloaded point by point for the capital of each of the 25 departments and for all 195 provinces; these series feed every territory card, the 1981-2010 baseline and the anomaly and Z-score calculation; (2) the live NASA POWER API, which the app itself calls for current conditions. GWETROOT also feeds the soil-stress term of the territorial risk score.
projectRefs: NOAA Oceanic Niño Index, https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/ensostuff/ONI_v4.shtml : defines the El Niño episode windows used for the historical comparisons.

IGP, Indice Costero El Nino (ICEN), https://www.igp.gob.pe/ : together with the ONI, it defines the coastal El Nino episode windows (for example, May 1997 to June 1998), so every historical comparison uses exactly the same window in every view of the app.
ENFEN, Comunicado Oficial N.° 20-2026, https://enfen.imarpe.gob.pe/downloads/comunicados/ : the official Peruvian Coastal El Niño alert behind the current period.
INEI, https://www.inei.gob.pe/ : official population projections shown in the department cards (for example, Lima: 11,298,944 people, with 8,135,240 in territory under alert in the current view).
Open-Meteo Weather API, https://open-meteo.com/ : current weather conditions (temperature, precipitation, relative humidity and wind) shown in the live mode of the app.
